denomProfiles/society-of-st-pius-x/tagli: Traditionalist priestly society founded by Archbishop Lefebvre to preserve the Tridentine Mass.
denomProfiles/society-of-st-pius-x/coreD: Catholic faith as taught before the Second Vatican Council, including papal primacy.
The 1962 Roman Missal and traditional rites as the full expression of the Catholic priesthood and sacrifice.
Rejection of Vatican II's teaching on religious liberty, ecumenism and collegiality as breaks with Tradition.
Recognition of the reigning Pope while refusing obedience in these matters; it is not sedevacantist.
denomProfiles/society-of-st-pius-x/focus: Training priests in its seminaries, beginning at Écône, Switzerland (1970).
Traditional Latin Mass in priories and chapels worldwide.
Catholic schools and traditional family life.
Doctrinal discussions with Rome on its canonical status.
denomProfiles/society-of-st-pius-x/pract: Mass in Latin according to the 1962 Missal, with Gregorian chant.
Confessions recognised as valid by Rome since 2015 and marriages under conditions since 2017.
denomProfiles/society-of-st-pius-x/influ: After the 1988 consecrations Rome set up the Fraternity of St Peter for traditionalists staying in communion.
Benedict XVI's freeing of the old Mass responded partly to the SSPX.
Priests who rejected the Society's recognition of the Pope left to form separate bodies.
denomProfiles/society-of-st-pius-x/keyFi: Founder; excommunicated after consecrating four bishops in 1988
denomProfiles/society-of-st-pius-x/inInd: The Society serves small traditionalist congregations in south India, chiefly in Tamil Nadu and Kerala, from its Asian District.
denomProfiles/philippine-independent-chu: Filipino nationalist church of catholic order, in full communion with Anglicans and Old Catholics.
The 1947 Declaration of Faith and Articles of Religion affirm the Trinity, the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds and the authority of Scripture.
Holds the historic episcopate, received from bishops of the US Episcopal Church in 1948, as essential to its catholic order.
Seven sacraments are retained, with baptism and the Eucharist treated as pre-eminent.
Teaches that the Church must be self-governing and rooted in Filipino culture rather than ruled by foreign clergy.
Understands the gospel as calling the Church to work for justice, human rights and the poor.
Filipino national identity and independence from foreign ecclesiastical control.
Social justice, labour rights and advocacy for peasants and indigenous peoples.
Ecumenical partnership with the Episcopal Church in the Philippines and the wider Anglican Communion.
Pastoral care of overseas Filipino workers and diaspora parishes.
Celebrates a catholic-style Mass, now largely in Filipino and other Philippine languages.
Clergy may marry; the church ordains women to the priesthood, a practice begun in the late 1990s.
Led by an elected Obispo Máximo (Supreme Bishop) and a synod-based episcopate.
Trains many of its clergy at St Andrew's Theological Seminary in Quezon City, shared with Philippine Episcopalians.
Honours the memory of Filipino patriots and clergy martyrs, such as the priests Gómez, Burgos and Zamora executed in 1872.
Episcopal Church in the Philippines
The two churches share a seminary, joint ministries and a long-standing concordat of full communion.
Philippine ecumenical social activism
Its bishops and clergy have been prominent in the National Council of Churches in the Philippines and human-rights campaigns.
Isabelo de los Reyes
Labour leader and journalist who proclaimed the church in 1902.
Gregorio Aglipay
Former Catholic priest and revolutionary chaplain; first Obispo Máximo (1902–40).
Isabelo de los Reyes Jr
Obispo Máximo who led the return to Trinitarian orthodoxy and the 1948 consecrations.
Alberto Ramento
Former Obispo Máximo and human-rights advocate, murdered in Tarlac in 2006.
denomProfiles/eastern-orthodox/tagline: Communion of self-governing churches keeping the faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
denomProfiles/eastern-orthodox/coreDoctr: Accepts the seven Ecumenical Councils (Nicaea 325 to Nicaea II 787) and the Nicene–Constantinopolitan Creed without the Filioque.
Holy Tradition, of which Scripture (with the Septuagint Old Testament) is the heart, is the rule of faith, interpreted by the Fathers and councils.
Salvation is theosis: participation in God's uncreated energies, while God's essence remains unknowable (Gregory Palamas, councils of 1341–51).
The veneration of icons is upheld as a confession of the Incarnation, celebrated on the Sunday of Orthodoxy (843).
The Church is a conciliar communion of local churches; the Ecumenical Patriarch holds a primacy of honour, not universal jurisdiction.
Mary is honoured as Theotokos and ever-virgin; the saints and the departed are commemorated in prayer.
denomProfiles/eastern-orthodox/focuses/0: The Divine Liturgy as the centre of church life and the experience of heaven on earth.
denomProfiles/eastern-orthodox/focuses/1: Monasticism, above all Mount Athos, as the spiritual heart of the Church.
denomProfiles/eastern-orthodox/focuses/2: Hesychast prayer and the Jesus Prayer, collected in the Philokalia (1782).
denomProfiles/eastern-orthodox/focuses/3: Continuity with the Church Fathers and resistance to doctrinal innovation.
denomProfiles/eastern-orthodox/focuses/4: Ecclesial unity across nations, despite recurring jurisdictional disputes.
denomProfiles/eastern-orthodox/practices: Celebrates the Liturgies of St John Chrysostom and St Basil in Greek, Church Slavonic, Arabic, Romanian and many vernaculars.
Baptises infants by triple immersion and immediately chrismates them and gives them Communion.
Keeps four fasting seasons and Wednesday and Friday fasts; Pascha is the feast of feasts.
Churches have an iconostasis; worshippers venerate icons, light candles and often stand.
Parish priests may marry before ordination; bishops are drawn from celibate monastics.
Some churches follow the Julian calendar, others the Revised Julian for fixed feasts, while all keep Pascha on the Julian reckoning (except Finland).
denomProfiles/eastern-orthodox/influence: The conversion of Kyivan Rus in 988 carried Byzantine Orthodoxy to the Slavic north.
Byzantine-rite Catholic churches keep Orthodox liturgy and spirituality in communion with Rome.
The mission of Cyril and Methodius created Slavonic literacy and the basis of the Cyrillic alphabet.
Émigré theologians such as Lossky and Florovsky influenced 20th-century Western theology and the World Council of Churches.
denomProfiles/eastern-orthodox/keyFigure: Archbishop of Constantinople whose liturgy is the Church's usual Eucharistic rite.
Systematiser of Orthodox doctrine and defender of icons.
Patriarch of Constantinople and critic of the Filioque in the 9th century.
Defender of hesychasm and the essence–energies distinction.
Theologian of the two wills of Christ and of deification.
denomProfiles/eastern-orthodox/members/n: Pew Research Center (2017) estimate of Orthodox Christians worldwide; this total also includes Oriental Orthodox churches such as the Ethiopian.
denomProfiles/eastern-orthodox/inIndia: Eastern Orthodoxy is very small in India; a few Indian communities are under the Ecumenical Patriarchate's Metropolis of Singapore and South Asia (created 2008). India's 'Orthodox' Christians in Kerala belong mainly to the Oriental Orthodox family instead.
denomProfiles/russian-orthodox/tagline: Largest Orthodox church, heir of the 988 baptism of Rus and of Moscow's patriarchate.
denomProfiles/russian-orthodox/coreDoctr: Shares the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils and the Creed without the Filioque.
Sees itself as the canonical church of the lands of historic Rus, including Russia, Belarus and (in its view) Ukraine.
Holds a strong theology of holy tradition, the saints and the New Martyrs of the Soviet era, canonised in large numbers in 2000.
Its 2000 'Bases of the Social Concept' sets out teaching on church–state relations, family, bioethics and war.
Emphasises church–state 'symphony' and a civilisational vision, recently expressed as the 'Russian world' (Russkii mir).
denomProfiles/russian-orthodox/focuses/0: Rebuilding parishes, monasteries and seminaries after Soviet persecution; tens of thousands of churches reopened after 1988.
denomProfiles/russian-orthodox/focuses/1: Monastic and elder (starets) spirituality, from Sergius of Radonezh to the Optina elders.
denomProfiles/russian-orthodox/focuses/2: Preserving Church Slavonic worship and the Julian calendar.
denomProfiles/russian-orthodox/focuses/3: A public role in Russian national life, which critics, including many Orthodox theologians, regard as too close to state power.
denomProfiles/russian-orthodox/practices: Long services in Church Slavonic, including the all-night vigil, with congregations usually standing.
Keeps the Julian calendar, celebrating Christmas on 7 January (civil calendar).
Rich traditions of icon painting (Andrei Rublev's Trinity) and bell-ringing.
Strict fasting before Communion and in the Great Fast; frequent confession before receiving.
Mass pilgrimages to relics and monasteries such as the Trinity–St Sergius Lavra.
denomProfiles/russian-orthodox/influence: Opponents of Patriarch Nikon's reforms broke away after the councils of 1666–67.
Grew from the Russian mission to Alaska (1794) and received autocephaly from Moscow in 1970.
Émigré bishops organised abroad after the revolution and reunited with Moscow in 2007.
Thinkers such as Khomyakov, Soloviev and Bulgakov drew on and reshaped Russian Orthodox thought.
denomProfiles/russian-orthodox/keyFigure: Prince of Kyiv whose baptism in 988 began the Christianisation of Rus.
14th-century monastic founder and Russia's best-loved saint.
Reformer of the 1650s whose liturgical changes provoked the Old Believer schism.
First patriarch after the restoration of 1917 and confessor under Soviet rule.
Patriarch since 2009, associated with the church's revival and with the 'Russian world' doctrine.
denomProfiles/russian-orthodox/members/n: Pew Research Center (2017) figure for Orthodox Christians in Russia, most of whom identify with the Moscow Patriarchate; the Patriarchate's own claims, which include Belarus, Ukraine and the diaspora, are much higher.
denomProfiles/ecumenical-patriarchate/ta: Historic see of New Rome, first in honour among Orthodox churches.
denomProfiles/ecumenical-patriarchate/co: Holds the full Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Claims, on the basis of canon 3 of Constantinople (381) and canon 28 of Chalcedon (451), a primacy of honour among Orthodox churches.
Teaches that it may hear appeals and grant autocephaly; this role is contested, especially by Moscow.
Asserts jurisdiction over the Orthodox diaspora outside the territories of other autocephalous churches.
Has championed the theological case for environmental care as a spiritual responsibility.
denomProfiles/ecumenical-patriarchate/fo: Pan-Orthodox coordination, culminating in the Holy and Great Council in Crete (2016).
Ecumenical dialogue, notably with Rome since Athenagoras and Paul VI lifted the 1054 anathemas in 1965.
Survival of a tiny Greek Orthodox community in Turkey and the reopening of the Halki seminary, closed in 1971.
Pastoral care of Greek-speaking and other diaspora churches in America, Britain and Australia.
Creation care, earning Patriarch Bartholomew the nickname 'Green Patriarch'.
denomProfiles/ecumenical-patriarchate/pr: The Patriarch resides at the Phanar in Istanbul, with the Patriarchal Church of St George.
Celebrates the Byzantine liturgy in its classical Greek form and Byzantine chant.
Follows the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts, adopted in 1923–24.
Oversees Mount Athos, the semi-autonomous Church of Crete, the Dodecanese and the autonomous churches of Finland and Estonia.
Turkish law requires the Patriarch to be a Turkish citizen, narrowing the pool of candidates.
denomProfiles/ecumenical-patriarchate/in: Constantinople sent the first metropolitans of Kyiv and recognised the Moscow patriarchate in 1589.
Granted autocephaly to the Greek church by Tomos in 1850.
Granted it a Tomos of autocephaly in January 2019.
The Kyivan metropolitanate that entered the Union of Brest (1596) had been under Constantinople.
denomProfiles/ecumenical-patriarchate/ke: Archbishop of Constantinople who presided briefly over the Council of 381.
Patriarch at the centre of the 9th-century dispute with Rome.
17th-century patriarch whose Calvinist-leaning Confession (1629) caused controversy.
Patriarch (1948–72) who met Pope Paul VI in Jerusalem in 1964.
Patriarch since 1991, active in ecumenism, environmentalism and the Ukrainian question.
